html:
Gap analysis turns approved requirements into build decisions: you compare each BrightLogistics requirement against out-of-the-box Salesforce, classify the difference, score its impact, and choose the most cost-effective resolution. By the end you will give every requirement a verdict — fit, partial, or no fit — with a defendable decision the team can build from.

Learning Objectives

  • Conduct a structured fit-gap assessment for every requirement in the backlog, ...
  • Classify each gap as configure, extend, third-party package, or custom build, ...
  • Score gaps by severity and frequency of business impact, ...
  • Write solution options with explicit trade-offs, ...
  • Document decisions in a solution design document, ...
  • Rank the gap backlog so the most painful gaps are resolved first, ...
  • Hand a traced fit-gap matrix forward into the UAT cycle, ...

1. What a Gap Means on a Salesforce Project

A gap is the difference between what the business needs and what the delivered platform does today — stock Salesforce plus the scratch org's configuration on a greenfield rollout like BrightLogistics, or the legacy system's exact behavior on a migration. Take each approved Business_Requirement__c record from Phase 4, compare it with platform capability, and record a verdict. Gaps come in three flavours:

Gap typeQuestion it answersBrightLogistics example
FunctionalDoes the platform do the action?Auto-assign each web lead to the right dispatcher
DataCan the platform store and relate the information?Store billing account alongside the freight quote
ProcessCan the workflow be expressed end to end?Two-level manager approval before a discounted quote ships

Run the analysis after approval and before build. The Process_Map__c records from Phase 3 feed it — as-is cycle times and step counts reveal how painful a gap is.

2. The Fit-Gap Matrix

The matrix has one row per requirement and one decision per row. The discipline: every row ends with a decision, never "we will think about it later."

md
Requirement                  | Fit                          | Gap                      | Decision
-----------------------------|------------------------------|--------------------------|--------------------------
Web lead capture             | Fit — Web-to-Lead            | None                     | Out-of-the-box
Auto-assign lead to dispatcher| Partial — assignment rules  | Needs routing by region  | Configure flow + queue
Digitized quote approval     | Partial — approval process  | Needs 2-level chain      | Configure approval process
Duplicate lead suppression   | Fit/partial — duplicate rules| Needs company+email match| Configure duplicate rule
Legacy billing integration   | No fit                       | Billing logic            | AppExchange or build
In-app customer chat         | No fit                       | Real-time messaging      | AppExchange package

Build it from the backlog, not memory. BrightLogistics runs a 60-minute fit-gap workshop after requirements review — the dispatcher SME confirms today's facts, Greg commercial priorities — then records every decision with a named owner.

3. Verdicts: Fit, Partial, No Fit

Every row gets exactly one verdict. The verdict is a statement about the platform, not about the value of the requirement:

VerdictMeaningBrightLogistics exampleDefault response
FitStandard Salesforce covers it as-isCapture web leads via Web-to-LeadUse it; no build
PartialMostly covered but needs configuration or light extensionLead routing needs region logicConfigure first, extend if needed
No fitNo standard or configurable support existsBilling engine for freight invoicingEvaluate a package, then build

A "fit" should be used, not embellished: when Web-to-Lead already turns a form into a Lead, do not surround it with redundant objects and rules. "Partial" is the most common verdict and where skill shows — that gap is where configure-vs-customize judgement is earned.

4. Where Gaps Really Come From

Before resolving a gap, record its source:

Source of gapDescriptionResponse
True platform limitSalesforce genuinely cannot express the behaviorExtend, package, or build
Legacy habitThe old process was this way because the old tool forced itChallenge with the business; usually drops out
MisunderstandingThe requirement is wrong or the team guessed wrongClarify, re-score, re-verify

Most "gaps" are habits: a brokerage that has typed leads into Excel for years will ask for "an Excel-like grid" because it is what they know. Separate the underlying need ("dispatchers must see and claim new work fast") from the mechanism ("in Excel").

5. The Resolution Ladder: Configure, Extend, Package, Build

Resolve gaps in cost-ascending order — the cheapest solution that fully closes the gap wins, and you escalate only when the cheaper rung cannot express the behavior:

  1. Configure — use stock Salesforce: objects, fields, picklists, validation rules, flows, approval processes, assignment rules, reports, dashboards. Lowest cost, free upgrades.
  2. Extend — add a thin layer of logic or integration: a service class, a trigger, a platform event, a callout. Costs more, stays close to the platform.
  3. Package — install a proven AppExchange solution. You pay licenses and gain vendor support, releases, and a roadmap maintained outside your team.
  4. Build — write and maintain the functionality yourself; the most expensive option for development, testing, and lifetime maintenance. Reserve it for when nothing else works, and say so in writing.

Treat it as a rule: skipping a rung takes on long-term cost without proving the lower rung impossible.

6. Configuration First

Configuration is the default answer for most BrightLogistics requirements:

Business needConfiguration
Web leads land as records automaticallyWeb-to-Lead, lead page layout, queue
Leads route to the right dispatcherAssignment rules + a routing flow, region-based
Discounted quotes need two bosses to approveApproval process with a 2-level step chain
Duplicate leads are suppressedDuplicate rule keyed on Email + Company
No quote ships without an ownerValidation rule on the Opportunity

Configuration is fast, cheap to maintain, and upgrade-compatible — a future release improves the configured solution with it, free. About two thirds of the BrightLogistics backlog resolves by configuration alone; the 80%-auto-assigned-in-60-days KPI needs assignment rules and one screen flow, no code.

7. Extend When Configuration Cannot Express Behavior

Configuration covers rules, routing, approvals, and screens — but not everything; then behavior needs a little platform code. This roadmap models extension the way a real team does: logic in service classes, thin trigger delegation, as in RequirementApprovalRoutingService.cls and UATDefectLoggerService.cls, plus the Requirement_Status_Changed__e platform event announcing state changes.

Extension is the right rung when:

  • The rule needs loops, callouts, or calculations configuration cannot express.
  • Behavior must react across objects (a requirement change rippling into story statuses).
  • An integration must speak an external API that flows cannot reach cleanly.

For BrightLogistics, small extension is justified for the billing handover if no package fits: an Apex service transforms a shipped Opportunity into the accounting payload while everything around it stays configured.

8. AppExchange — Reuse Before You Build

AppExchange is Salesforce's marketplace of pre-built solutions; a package often closes a "no fit" gap in days, not months. "It will not be exactly what we want" applies to your own code too — the question is whether a 90% fit plus vendor support beats a 100% fit plus your full-time maintenance.

CriterionWhat to checkBrightLogistics example
Fit of the core flowDoes it solve the actual business problem?Live chat connects to the Lead record
Security reviewHas it passed AppExchange security review?Yes / status visible on listing
Reviews and installsWhat do similar-size companies say?Ratings, install count
Pricing and license modelPer-user, per-org, one-time?Cost inside the rollout budget
Support and roadmapWho answers tickets, how fast?Vendor SLA and release cadence

Record the comparison — options, scores, deciders — in the design document.

9. Custom Build — The Last Resort

A custom build is not forbidden — it is expensive to own. The build invoice is the smallest cost you will ever pay: every upgrade, patch, and new hire inherits lifetime maintenance. The design document must state in writing why build beats the alternatives.

Custom build earns its place when:

  • The gap is genuinely core to the business (competitive advantage, not nice-to-have).
  • No package exists, or the existing packages fail the security, pricing, or support bar.

Nothing at BrightLogistics yet justifies a full build — the billing handover suits extension or a package. The honesty test: if Greg asked "why did we build this?" and the answer was not three sentences, the decision was too fast.

10. Scoring Gaps: Severity and Frequency

Two independent numbers describe how much a gap hurts:

  • Severity (1–5): business impact if unresolved — 1 = cosmetic, 5 = blocks operations.
  • Frequency (1–5): how often the pain occurs — 1 = rare edge case, 5 = every working day.

Their product is the pain and drives resolution order. GapAnalysisService.cls computes it on the requirement record:

apex
// GapAnalysisService fits each requirement vs the platform.
// Severity: 1 (cosmetic) .. 5 (blocks business)   Frequency: 1..5
// Impact = Severity * Frequency -> drives the design decision rank.
for (Business_Requirement__c r : [SELECT Id, Severity__c, Frequency__c
                                  FROM Business_Requirement__c
                                  WHERE Gap_Score__c = null]) {
  Integer gapImpact = Integer.valueOf(r.Severity__c)
                    * Integer.valueOf(r.Frequency__c);
  r.Gap_Score__c = gapImpact;   // 25 = must resolve, 1 = accept as-is
}

Reading the score tells you what happens next:

SeverityFrequencyScoreMeaning
5525Blocks the business, every day — resolve immediately
5210Severe but rare — schedule it, do not ignore it
2510Mild but constant — quality-of-life fix, cheap to ship
111Cosmetic and rare — accept as-is, document the decision

11. Ranking the Gap Backlog

Rank by Gap_Score__c and apply common sense — scores do not build the release plan, people do:

RequirementSeverityFrequencyGap scoreResolutionSprint
Auto-assign web leads to the right dispatcher5525Configure assignment + flowSprint 1
Digitized two-level quote approval4416Configure approval processSprint 1
Duplicate lead suppression3515Configure duplicate ruleSprint 2
Legacy billing handover4312Evaluate package / extendSprint 3
Customer chat326Package evaluationBacklog
  • Score 16+ (severe × constant) moves into the first sprints and has an owner.
  • Score 6–15 is planned explicitly and assigned a decision date.
  • Score 5 and below is accepted as-is — and that acceptance is written down, because acceptance is itself a decision.

Value_Score__c breaks ties between equal gap scores. Re-run the ranking at every sprint review. Exercise 7.3 in the Phase 15 guide drills it from scratch.

12. Writing the Solution Design Document

The solution design document is the delivery contract: requirements plus decisions. Without the reasoning it is a shopping list; with it, the document survives audits and "why did we do it this way?" reviews.

A useful structure:

  1. Executive summary and the non-negotiables (the two KPI targets).
  2. Fit-gap matrix — every requirement with verdict and score.
  3. Decisions log — one entry per gap with options and trade-offs.
  4. Solution overview — object model, automation, and reports touched.
  5. Assumptions, dependencies, and open questions carried from the BRD.

Each decision entry is a small table:

FieldValue
Decision IDD-104
RequirementSuppress duplicate leads (R-104)
OptionsDuplicate rule vs build a merge utility
Trade-offRule is free and upgrade-safe; merge utility is heavier than the need
DecisionConfigure the duplicate rule
Decided byOps lead, confirmed by sponsor

The Requirement_Approval_Routing approval process (see Phase 9) gates acceptance — "Approved" requires criteria filled. Revisited decisions add a new row, never an edit, so history stays honest.

13. From Fit-Gap to UAT

The matrix is the input to the next phases: configure decisions become stories with criteria, extend and build decisions carry size and test notes, package decisions become installation work. The traceability chain stays intact.

The ranked list tells UAT what to prove: highest-scored gaps become priority scenarios in Phase 12, and the decisions feed Phase 13. At the end the BA holds four artifacts — the fit-gap matrix, the ranked backlog, the decisions log, and the design document — the deliverables Exercise 7.3 checks and the raw material for Exercises 9.1 and 9.2.

Hands-On Exercises

1. BrightLogistics Fit-Gap Matrix

Build the fit-gap matrix for the lead-intake backlog.

Steps:

  1. List six requirements from the BRD (capture, routing, approval, duplicates, billing, reporting).
  2. Score each row Fit / Partial / No fit and describe the gap precisely.
  3. Write the decision for each row and name the stakeholder who owns it.

Expected result: a six-row matrix where every row has a verdict, a gap description, and an owner.

What it proves: that fit-gap demands explicit decisions.

2. Score the Gaps with Severity and Frequency

Apply the scoring model to your matrix.

Steps:

  1. Give every gap a Severity (1–5) and Frequency (1–5).
  2. Compute Gap_Score__c = Severity × Frequency for each.
  3. Sort by score and defend the top three sprint choices.

Expected result: a ranked list with scores and a defendable sprint assignment.

What it proves: that Gap_Score__c turns subjective pain into an orderable backlog.

3. Resolution Ladder Memo

Write a one-page decision memo for the billing-handover gap.

Steps:

  1. State the requirement and the "no fit" verdict.
  2. List all four ladder options with a one-line trade-off each.
  3. Recommend one option and justify the choice.

Expected result: a memo a sponsor can approve in one reading.

What it proves: that the configure → extend → package → build ladder forces cost-ascending thinking.

4. Design Decision Record

Produce the decisions log for the gaps in exercises 1–2.

Steps:

  1. Create one decision row per gap with ID, options, trade-off, and decision.
  2. Mark who decided and the approval status.
  3. Cross-check that every decision maps to a requirement ID.

Expected result: a complete D-101..D-106 log with no orphan decisions.

What it proves: that the design document is traceable backward to requirements and forward to UAT.

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
GapThe difference between a business need and current platform capability
Fit-gap matrixA per-requirement table comparing need vs capability, one decision per row
Config vs customizeThe cost-ascending choice between stock features and built code
ConfigureResolving a gap with stock platform features (objects, flows, approvals)
ExtendAdding a thin layer of Apex or integration on top of configuration
AppExchangeSalesforce's marketplace of pre-built, reviewed solutions
Custom buildWriting and maintaining functionality yourself; highest lifetime cost
SeverityBusiness impact of an unresolved gap, scored 1–5
FrequencyHow often the gap's pain occurs, scored 1–5
Gap_Score__cThe impact product of severity and frequency on Business_Requirement__c
Decision logThe record of choices, trade-offs, and owners per gap
Give each gap a verdictThe statement that the platform fits, partially fits, or does not fit a need
Accepted as-isA documented decision to leave a low-impact gap unresolved

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can run a fit-gap workshop and produce one decision per requirement row.
  • I can explain why configuration precedes every other resolution option.
  • I can evaluate an AppExchange package against five named criteria.
  • I can compute and interpret Gap_Scorec from Severityc and Frequency__c.
  • I can write a design document where every decision has trade-offs and an owner.
  • I can trace a fit-gap decision into a user story and a UAT test case.
  • I have completed Exercise 7.3 (Fit-Gap Verdicts) in Phase 15.

Summary

You learned that gap analysis converts a requirement backlog into a ranked set of build decisions. You read every requirement through a fit-gap matrix with three verdicts, resolve gaps up the configure → extend → package → build ladder, and score the pain each gap causes using severity times frequency on the Business_Requirement__c record. The design document records those decisions with trade-offs and owners, and the same matrix hands a ranked list of scenarios forward into UAT.
